name: FDIC Branch
description: A 90-minute, 4-round Express simulation on managing a US retail-bank branch under federal regulation, for money-and-banking, financial-institutions management and business-law courses at Hispanic-Serving Institutions, personal-banker certificates and community-bank management-trainee programmes. Bilingual EN/ES. Sonoran Ridge Community Bank (a fictional FDIC-supervised state bank in Arizona): as the new manager of its Maryvale branch in Phoenix, with about 180 million dollars of deposits, you run the branch through 2027. You decide the bankers incentive plan and language access for Spanish-speaking customers, loan-pricing exceptions and the Community Reinvestment Act lending plan, how to handle a cash-structuring pattern and a depositor asking about FDIC insurance, and whether to close a satellite office and how to remediate accounts opened without consent. Scored on branch contribution, compliance findings, the CRA index and households served.
view:
FDIC Branch

Your first year as manager of a community bank’s branch in Maryvale, Phoenix: set the sales plan, serve the neighbourhood in its language, price loans fairly, lend in the tracts the Community Reinvestment Act measures, report cash honestly, explain deposit insurance, decide the satellite office and clean up the accounts nobody asked for.

Sonoran Ridge Community Bank · Maryvale, Phoenix, Arizona · the branch manager You are Marisol Quintero Ybarra, 36, a former personal banker who grew up in Maryvale and who on Monday 4 January 2027 takes over Sonoran Ridge Community Bank’s branch on West Indian School Road and its small satellite office on 35th Avenue. The bank has an Arizona state charter and is not a Federal Reserve member, so its federal supervisor is the FDIC. The branch has 16 employees, about $180 million of deposits and $55 million of loans; in 2026 it earned about $5.6 million (the funds-transfer-pricing credit on its deposits, the spread on its loans and fees) and left a contribution of about $900,000. Most of the census tracts it serves are low- or moderate-income and about two in three households speak Spanish at home. The FDIC evaluates the bank under the Community Reinvestment Act in November 2027. Every round is measured on the decisions taken so far.

Round 1 · Monday 4 January 2027: the sales plan and the language of service

Craig Ostrander’s 2027 retail plan doubles the account-opening goals and asks every branch for a Spanish-language campaign for the free checking account. The six personal bankers’ incentive plan: keep the bank’s product-count goals with monthly payouts per account opened (volume +2%; half a finding; $30,000 more exposure for unauthorized accounts); a scorecard that pays on balances still active after 90 days, customer surveys and a compliance quality check, with clawback of incentives for accounts closed unused or opened without consent ($60,000 for the reviews and the redesign; volume +1%; households +3); salary only, no incentives (volume −2%); or the regional plan — double the goals, a daily leaderboard and performance plans for bankers below target (volume +4%; $20,000 of contests; 1 finding; households −3; $110,000 more exposure). Language: service and documents in English with a telephone interpreter on request; a written language-access policy with two certified bilingual bankers, a bilingual teller on every shift, the account agreement and key disclosures in Spanish and complaints taken in Spanish ($70,000; volume +3%; CRA index +6; households +4); the Spanish radio and billboard campaign with English-only staff and documents ($25,000; volume +2%; 1 finding; households −2); or steer customers to the app and close the teller line on Saturdays (saves $90,000; volume −1%; CRA index −6; households −3).

Opening accounts or cards without the customer’s consent is an unfair and abusive practice (12 U.S.C. §§ 5531, 5536). Advertising in Spanish a service delivered only in English can mislead customers.

Round 2 · Monday 5 April 2027: loan pricing and the CRA lending plan

On Tuesday 16 February the review of the branch’s 2026 HMDA data showed that the loan officers’ discretionary pricing exceptions left Hispanic borrowers on average 0.30 percentage points worse off than non-Hispanic white borrowers with similar credit, and that the branch’s own tracts had fewer mortgage applications than any other branch’s. Pricing: leave the discretion as it is (1 finding; CRA index −2); a written rate sheet, exceptions only for documented reasons (a competing offer in writing, relationship balances), a second review of every exception and a monthly comparison by HMDA group ($20,000; CRA index +2; households +1); centralised pricing with no exceptions at all ($10,000; volume −2%); or a 680 minimum credit score and no mortgage or small-business loan under $100,000 (saves $15,000; volume −1%; half a finding; CRA index −10; households −2). The CRA plan: none; a first-time homebuyer programme with down-payment grants through the Federal Home Loan Bank, homebuyer education in Spanish with Casa Adelante, a HUD-approved counselling agency, and SBA-guaranteed microloans to Maryvale businesses ($90,000 including higher provisions; volume +2%; CRA index +14; households +3); buy $4 million of CRA-qualifying mortgages originated by another lender ($30,000 of yield given up; CRA index +6); or move the loan officer and the mailers to the higher-income ZIP codes outside Maryvale (saves $20,000; volume +1%; 2 findings; about $50,000 as the branch’s share of a redlining settlement; CRA index −12; households −3).

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act forbids discrimination on national origin in any credit transaction (15 U.S.C. § 1691). The CRA measures how a bank meets the credit needs of its whole community, including low- and moderate-income neighbourhoods (12 U.S.C. §§ 2901–2908).

Round 3 · Tuesday 6 July 2027: the cash and the insurance

On Thursday 20 May, Arturo Celaya, owner of Carnicería El Saguaro, deposited $9,500 in cash for the fourth time in two weeks, after asking a teller what happens above $10,000. In June, Efraín Ledesma, 67, a customer for thirty years, sold his tire shop for $780,000 and asks you whether “all of it” will be FDIC insured at the branch. Arturo’s cash: nothing — he is a good customer and no deposit reaches $10,000 (about $20,000 of exam remediation; 1 finding); tellers aggregate same-day cash for the currency transaction reports, the pattern goes to Denise Okafor-Hale, the BSA officer, who decides on a suspicious activity report, nobody tells the customer and the branch keeps serving the business while updating its cash profile ($5,000); close his account and tell him it is because of the reports (volume −0.5%; 1.5 findings; households −2); or a teller tells him to keep each deposit under $10,000 “so there is no paperwork” (about $40,000; 3 findings). The Ledesmas’ $780,000: send them to the brokerage partner or tell him to spread it across banks himself (volume −0.5%); explain coverage by ownership category with the FDIC’s estimator — $250,000 in his name, $250,000 in his wife Rosaura’s name and $280,000 in a joint account, $140,000 for each co-owner, all insured — and put it in writing ($5,000; volume +0.5%; households +2); tell him “everything here is FDIC insured” and open one account in his name (1.5 findings; households −1); or one $780,000 certificate of deposit in his name without discussing the limit, leaving $530,000 uninsured (half a finding; households −1).

Breaking up cash deposits to avoid the $10,000 report is a federal crime for the customer and for anyone who helps (31 U.S.C. § 5324): it caps the score at 35. The FDIC insures up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each ownership category (12 CFR Part 330).

Round 4 · Monday 4 October 2027: the satellite office and the audit

On Monday 23 August regional proposed closing the 35th Avenue office, used by about 1,900 households in a moderate-income tract. On Wednesday 15 September internal audit found personal accounts and debit cards opened in 2025–2027 without customers’ signatures by two bankers chasing the goals; the exposure starts at $40,000 and grows with the 2027 incentive plan. The office: close it with the 90-day notice to the FDIC and to customers, a notice posted in the office 30 days before and the ATM kept (saves $180,000; volume −2%; CRA index −8; households −3); keep it with shorter hours, an interactive teller machine and a bilingual banker three days a week ($60,000; CRA index +6; households +2); close it in 30 days with a letter, without the 90-day notice (saves $190,000; about $25,000 of remediation; 1.5 findings; CRA index −12; households −5); or convert it to a full-service branch ($220,000; volume +2%; CRA index +8; households +3). The accounts nobody asked for: fire the two bankers and refund the fees the audit found (0.6 times the exposure plus $10,000; 1 finding); close every unauthorized account, refund all fees with interest, review every banker, correct affected credit reports, report it through the bank’s compliance and complaint process and change the incentive (the full exposure plus $30,000; households +1); close them quietly with no refunds and no report (0.3 times; 2 findings; households −3); or keep them open and reclassify them as customer-requested to protect the branch’s numbers (2.5 times; 3 findings; households −4).

An insured bank must notify its supervisor and its customers at least 90 days before closing a branch (12 U.S.C. § 1831r-1). Keeping unauthorized accounts open and falsifying their origin is fraud: it caps the score at 35.

summary.en: You are Marisol Quintero Ybarra, new manager of the Maryvale branch in Phoenix of Sonoran Ridge Community Bank, an FDIC-supervised Arizona bank. With about 180 million dollars in deposits, you set banker incentives, Spanish-language service and CRA lending, and handle compliance red flags.
summary.es: Eres Marisol Quintero Ybarra, nueva directora de la sucursal de Maryvale en Phoenix de Sonoran Ridge Community Bank, banco de Arizona supervisado por la FDIC. Con unos 180 millones de dólares en depósitos, fijas incentivos, atención en español y crédito CRA, y gestionas alertas de cumplimiento.

text.en: Analyze a branch's contribution from its deposit credit, loan spread, fees and costs, and trace which decisions move volume, cost, compliance findings and households served
text.es: Analizar la contribución de una sucursal a partir del crédito por depósitos, el diferencial de los préstamos, las comisiones y los costes, y seguir qué decisiones mueven el volumen, el coste, los hallazgos de cumplimiento y los hogares atendidos

text.en: Design a banker incentive plan that meets lending targets without producing accounts nobody asked for, alongside loan pricing on documented criteria, honest cash reporting and accurate deposit-insurance explanations
text.es: Diseñar un plan de incentivos para los banqueros que cumpla los objetivos sin generar cuentas que nadie pidió, junto con precios de préstamos según criterios documentados, reportes de efectivo honestos y explicaciones exactas del seguro de depósitos

text.en: Apply Community Reinvestment Act goals by lending, serving and keeping offices in low- and moderate-income tracts, and close a branch only by the rules
text.es: Aplicar los objetivos de la Community Reinvestment Act prestando, atendiendo y manteniendo oficinas en los sectores de ingresos bajos y moderados, y cerrar una sucursal solo según las reglas

text.en: Apply fair-service principles to a Spanish-speaking community, planning language access and never marketing what the branch cannot deliver in Spanish
text.es: Aplicar principios de servicio justo a una comunidad hispanohablante, planificando el acceso lingüístico y sin anunciar nunca lo que la sucursal no puede ofrecer en español

text.en: Evaluate how to remediate a sales-conduct failure, repaying customers, ending the practice and reporting it instead of firing the people involved and hiding the rest
text.es: Evaluar cómo remediar una falla de conducta comercial, devolviendo el dinero a los clientes, terminando la práctica e informándola en lugar de despedir a los implicados y ocultar el resto
